lesson.title: When Rate Depends on Concentration Squared: The Second-Order Integrated Law
lesson.summary: Derives the reciprocal relationship that connects concentration and time for a second order reaction, and shows why its half-life, unlike first order's, keeps changing as the reaction proceeds.
lesson.body:
A second order reaction has a differential rate law that depends on [A] squared, rate = k[A]^2 (or, for a reaction that is first order in each of two different reactants, rate = k[A][B]; this section focuses on the single-reactant case). Integrating that differential equation does not produce a logarithm the way the first order case did. Squaring the concentration in the rate law changes the shape of the calculus problem, and the result comes out as a reciprocal relationship instead.

The second order integrated rate law is:

1/[A] = 1/[A]0 + kt

where [A]0 is the initial concentration, [A] is the concentration at time t, and k is the second order rate constant, with units of inverse concentration times inverse time, such as M^-1 min^-1 or L mol^-1 min^-1 (notice these units are different from first order's k, a useful way to identify order just from the units given in a problem). This equation is also a straight line in disguise: if y = 1/[A] and x = t, then the slope is +k (positive, in contrast to first order's negative slope when ln[A] is plotted against t) and the intercept is 1/[A]0.

Worked example: a second order reaction has k = 0.250 M^-1 min^-1 and starts at [A]0 = 0.400 M. What is [A] after 10.0 minutes?

1/[A] = 1/0.400 + (0.250)(10.0)
1/[A] = 2.50 + 2.50
1/[A] = 5.00 M^-1

[A] = 1/5.00 = 0.200 M

So after 10.0 minutes the concentration has fallen from 0.400 M to exactly 0.200 M, precisely half. That is worth pausing on, because it lets us compute the second order half-life directly. Setting [A] = [A]0/2 in the integrated rate law and solving for t1/2 gives t1/2 = 1/(k[A]0). Plugging in this example's numbers: t1/2 = 1/(0.250 x 0.400) = 1/0.100 = 10.0 min, which matches the 10.0 minute result above exactly, a good internal check that the algebra is consistent.

Notice what is sitting inside that half-life formula: [A]0, the starting concentration, appears explicitly. That is the single most important fact to take away from second order kinetics, and it stands in direct contrast to first order behavior, which you will see formalized in the next two sections. For a second order reaction, a more concentrated starting point produces a shorter first half-life, and as the reaction proceeds and [A] keeps dropping, each successive half-life takes longer than the one before it, because the current, ever-shrinking concentration is what goes into the formula each time. First order half-life, by contrast, never changes no matter how much or how little reactant remains, which is exactly the property that makes it useful enough to deserve its own dedicated treatment next.
